body_markdown:
You're on the line at an indoor range, four hours into qualification. Your earmuff cushion has been riding on your eye protection arms since the first relay, so one side of your head has never sealed your ear properly. Your radio earpiece sits in your left ear, and nothing at all covers that ear. After your shooting session, you’ve got this faint ringing in your ears for hours, and you wonder if you’ve done some real damage to your hearing.


Problems like these call for tactical hearing protection. Hearing protection gear that you have to take off or leave off can affect your permanent hearing in years to come.


Duty situation What hearing protection gear works Why


Indoor qualification, braked rifles, shooters on both sides Electronic earplugs worn under earmuffs Doubling up your hearing protection gear adds measurable peak sound reduction where impulse levels run highest


Range instruction, hours on the line Electronic earmuffs Comfortable across long days, and range commands stay audible between strings


Under a helmet, or alongside a radio earpiece Electronic earplugs No earmuff cup to fight your helmet strap or your comms wire


Patrol, where loud noise arrives unplanned Earplugs carried on your person Protection in your pocket beats protection in your locker


Long days in heat and sweat Sweat-rated electronic earbuds A water and dust resistance rating decides whether your earbuds survive the summer


## Range Noise and Patrol Noise Need Different Hearing Protection


Duty noise comes in two kinds: Range noise is concentrated, predictable, and extreme. Patrol noise is scattered and arrives without notice. One pair of hearing protection rarely serves both situations well.


### Range Noise Concentrates a Whole Year of Noise Exposure Into a Few Days


The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) reports that[firearms produce impulses above the 140 decibel occupational limit, often reaching 160 to 170 decibels at the peak.](https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/bulletin/2017/firearms-training.html) An indoor range makes impulse noise worse because hard walls and a low ceiling send the explosive noise back at everyone on the line instead of letting it disperse.


How often you stand in the middle of that noise depends on your assignment. NIOSH estimates that a patrol officer is on a range about four times a year, a special team member is on a range about once a month, and a firearms instructor is on a range up to twenty times a month.


A firearms instructor spends hundreds of hours a year beside shooters and takes on more cumulative gunshot sound exposure than any officer being trained.


Range noise calls for the highest hearing protection rating. If you’re a firearms instructor, you need hearing protection gear that’s comfortable enough to stay on from the first relay to the last.


### Patrol Noise Arrives Without Warning and Rarely Repeats


Patrol noise usually involves sirens, traffic, a door coming down and, on rare days, a gunshot discharge nobody plans for. Most officers don't wear hearing protection on patrol, because a patrol needs situational awareness before loud sounds become an issue.


That is where electronic hearing protection beats a passive earplug. Electronic hearing protection compresses harmful impulse noises while amplifying the low-level sounds you still need to hear, so you can wear your protection gear through a whole patrol and not lose audio details between incidents.


Both kinds of noise need to reach your ears while your radio is running.


## Ear Protection With Comms: Three Setups Compared


Three setups put radio or phone audio alongside hearing protection, and each setup suits a different assignment.


Setup What it carries Best suited to


A dedicated comms headset with a radio interface Duty radio traffic, with push-to-talk on the headset Tactical teams whose radio traffic runs continuously


Electronic hearing protection worn with your issued radio earpiece Protection and hearing enhancement in both ears, with your radio setup unchanged Patrol officers and instructors who already carry an earpiece


Bluetooth hearing protection paired to your phone Calls, coordination, and hearing enhancement, with no extra wire running into your vest Training days, range instruction and general duty


Most officers end up in the middle setup. A radio earpiece sits in one ear and covers nothing, so that ear takes every round fired on the line at full level.


**Tip:** On a range, take your radio earpiece out and put hearing protection in both ears before the line goes hot.


The third setup pairs your hearing protection with your phone instead of your radio. Bluetooth hearing protection handles calls, coordination, and hearing enhancement while your issued earpiece carries radio traffic, so the two can run side by side on training days, on the range, and through general patrol.


It’s important to note that Bluetooth hearing protection is not a substitute for an issued radio interface. Bluetooth hearing protection handles phone calls, coordination, and hearing enhancement but cannot connect to your duty radio.


Whatever setup you run for comms, your radio is only one of two things fighting for space around your ears.


## Does Hearing Protection Work Under a Tactical Helmet?


Your helmet is the second thing fighting for that space, and yes, hearing protection works under a tactical helmet. Which type you wear decides how much of your rating survives the helmet.


### A Helmet Retention Strap Lifts an Earmuff Cushion Off Your Head


An earmuff protects your hearing by having an unbroken seal between the earmuff cushion and your head. A chin strap or a rear retention strap of your helmet may cross the earmuff cushion line, and the helmet strap can lift the cushion off your skin. Rail-mounted earmuffs exist for this reason, since mounting the cups to the helmet keeps the straps out from under the cushion.


### Earplugs Sit Where Your Helmet Can't Reach Them


Earplugs sit inside your ear canal, so your helmet has nothing to press against and your hearing protection seal doesn't depend on how your helmet is adjusted. For people who wear a helmet regularly, in-ear hearing protection is the best fit.


### Your Eye Protection Breaks the Same Hearing Protection Seal


The arms on your safety glasses can run between your earmuff cushion and your head, and any gap along that line costs you the protection you paid for.


Your vest collar, your radio wire, and your helmet's rear cradle can each push an earmuff cup off center or hold the cup away from your neck.


**Tip:** If you wear earmuffs with safety glasses, choose glasses with thin, straight arms, and press each cushion down over the arm after you seat your earmuffs.


### Heat and Sweat Are Factors For Ear Protection In The Summer


Earmuff cushions hold sweat against your head, and sweat breaks down the foam that makes the seal work. An ingress protection rating, written as IP followed by two digits, tells you how much dust and water a product is built to take.


Fit problems like these change what a hearing protection rating is worth to you, so the number on the box, and the phrase printed beside the number, both deserve a closer look.


## Military Grade Hearing Protection: What the Ratings Mean


The phrase printed beside those numbers is usually "military grade," and no certification, test, or standard sits behind the phrase. Any brand can print "military grade" on a box.


### NRR and SNR Are the Hearing Protection Ratings With Testing Behind Them


The Noise Reduction Rating comes from American National Standards Institute (ANSI) testing in the United States. The Single Number Rating comes from EN 352 testing in Europe. You'll often see both ratings printed on the same package of hearing protection gear.


Both figures come from a laboratory fit, and your fit is the one you get on duty. OSHA's noise standard caps impulse noise at 140 decibels peak, a ceiling every duty firearm clears.[OSHA also states that a hearing protector's rating doesn't always reflect the actual level of protection](https://www.osha.gov/otm/section-3-health-hazards/chapter-5) , because most wearers are never fit tested.


### Is 32 dB NRR Good for Shooting?


A 32 dB NRR sits near the top of what any single protector is rated for, and a 32 dB NRR covers a pistol or carbine line comfortably. Run your safety glasses arms under the cushion, though, and a 32 rating can drop well below 32, with no way for you to know by how much. You can read more about this in our[guide to how NRR ratings work](https://goaxil.com/blogs/axil/nrr-rating-for-shooting-everything-you-need-to-know-axil) .


Duty situation What to aim for Why


Outdoor qualification, pistol and carbine One well-sealed protector you keep on for the whole relay A seal you hold all day beats a higher rating you break between strings


Indoor qualification, braked rifles, shooters on both sides Earplugs under earmuffs Reflected impulse energy reaches you from more directions than your own muzzle


Range instruction across full days Electronic earmuffs, with earplugs added underneath during live fire Instructor exposure accumulates across a year, not across a session


Patrol and general duty Electronic in-ear protection you can leave in Hearing enhancement keeps protection from costing you awareness


Any assignment where you can't predict the noise Earplugs you carry on your person A rating is worth nothing if the protection is in your locker


## AXIL Tactical Hearing Protection Options for Duty Use


Every option below compresses sound above 85 decibels and amplifies what sits under that threshold, so your choice comes down to form factor, runtime, and weather resistance. Ratings appear as both a Noise Reduction Rating and a Single Number Rating, and the full range can be found in[our military and law enforcement collection](https://goaxil.com/collections/military-and-law-enforcement) .


### XCOR PRO: The In-Ear Option for Helmets and Radio Earpieces


The[XCOR PRO](https://goaxil.com/products/xcor) is rated 27 to 29 dB SNR and 21 to 23 dB NRR depending on which ear tips you fit, with foam tips giving you the higher figure. You get up to 13 hours of hearing protection and audio enhancement on one charge, or about 5 hours with Bluetooth 5.2 running alongside. The charging case takes USB-C.


Best for: officers who wear a helmet regularly, and anyone already running a radio earpiece who needs the other ear covered properly.


### GS Extreme 3.0: The Option Built for Heat and Long Days


The[GS Extreme 3.0 electronic earbuds](https://goaxil.com/products/gs-extreme-3-0) carry an IP65 dust and water resistance rating, which is great for hearing protection that needs to survive a summer of outdoor duty. Foam tips are rated 26 dB SNR and 21 dB NRR. You get up to 40 hours of hearing enhancement, or up to 15 hours with Bluetooth 5.3 and enhancement running together.


Best for: long outdoor days where you need one charge to cover the whole assignment.


### MX PRO and MX II PRO: The Over-Ear Options for Range Instruction


The[MX PRO earmuffs](https://goaxil.com/products/mx-pro) are rated 30 dB SNR and run up to 70 hours of hearing enhancement, which covers weeks of instruction between charges. The[MX II PRO earmuffs](https://goaxil.com/products/mxii-pro) are rated 22 dB NRR, carry an IP65 rating, and store a pair of AXIL earplugs in a compartment built into the earmuffs, so your second layer travels with your first.


Best for: firearms instructors and anyone running qualification days from the line instead of the firing point.


### SIG SAUER TRACKR Blu: The Option That Runs on AAA Batteries


The[SIG SAUER TRACKR Blu earmuffs](https://goaxil.com/products/sig-sauer-trackr-blu) are rated 27 dB SNR and run on two AAA batteries instead of a charge cycle. Autoblocker compression engages above 85 decibels and reacts in 0.02 seconds.


Best for: kit bags and patrol vehicles where a flat battery has to be a two-minute fix.


### X30i: The Option With No Battery at All


The[X30i earplugs](https://goaxil.com/products/x30i-earplugs) use a mechanical toggle to switch between full protection and hear-through, with no electronics and no charging involved. Foam tips are rated 19 dB NRR in closed mode, with 31 dB of impulse peak reduction under the IPIL standard.


Best for: the pair that lives in your kit bag for exposure you didn't plan for.


An individual officer makes that choice once. An agency makes the choice for everyone on the roster, and that brings a different set of questions.


## Six Questions to Ask Before Specifying a Tactical Hearing Protection System


Six questions decide whether a unit specification turns into protection your people will wear:


1. What is the real annual exposure by assignment, counting instructors separately from patrol officers?
2. What does the hearing protection gear need to work alongside? Specifically which helmet, which eye protection, and which radio?
3. How is each pair cleaned, and is any pair shared between officers across relays?
4. What is the charging plan across a unit, and what should an officer do if their battery dies in the middle of duty?
5. What is the replacement cycle for ear tips and earmuff cushions, which wear out faster than the electronics do?
6. How many sizes does the specification cover?


Ear canals and head shapes vary widely across any roster, and a program that issues one model in one size to everybody is giving real protection to some officers and a partial seal to the rest. Fit testing, or at minimum a choice of ear tip sizes and materials, turns a specification into protection your people will wear.


Hearing loss accumulates over a career, and an officer rarely notices the problem until conversations start getting harder to follow.


AXIL works with agencies and units on specification, sizing and volume orders, and you can contact the AXIL team directly for unit enquiries.


## Common Questions About Military and Police Hearing Protection


What hearing protection does the military use?


Issued protection generally falls into three categories: passive earplugs, level-dependent electronic earplugs that let low-level sound through while compressing loud sound, and tactical communication headsets that carry radio traffic through the hearing protection. Which category a service member receives depends on their role and their unit, not on a single standard-issue item.


What do Navy SEALs or special forces use for ear protection?


Special operations units typically run tactical communication headsets or in-ear systems with a radio interface, because comms and protection have to work as one piece of equipment for these units. Specific procurement varies by unit and isn't published in useful detail, so treat any brand claim about special operations issue with skepticism unless a contract backs the claim.


Do police officers wear hearing protection on patrol?


Most officers don't. Hearing protection is standard for qualification, firearms training and range instruction, and protection is uncommon on patrol because officers need full situational awareness through a whole tour. Electronic in-ear protection is the option that covers both, since electronic in-ear protection amplifies low-level sound and compresses sudden impulses.


Can you use tactical hearing protection with a radio?


Yes. A dedicated comms headset connects to your duty radio directly, and electronic hearing protection works alongside an issued radio earpiece as long as the radio ear is protected too. Bluetooth hearing protection pairs with your phone, which covers calls and coordination while your earpiece carries radio traffic.


How long does electronic hearing protection run on one charge?


It depends on what you have switched on. Hearing enhancement alone draws the least, and running Bluetooth audio at the same time roughly halves the figure on most models. AXIL's current earbuds and earmuffs range from about 13 hours to about 70 hours on enhancement alone, which is why runtime is worth checking against your longest duty day instead of your average one.


What NRR do you need for duty firearms training?


A well-sealed protector in the low to mid twenties covers most outdoor pistol and carbine qualification. Indoor ranges and braked rifles call for earplugs under earmuffs instead of a higher single rating. The guide to how NRR ratings work goes through the arithmetic.


## Making Tactical Hearing Protection Part of Your Duty Kit


Three things turn a new purchase into gear you wear every day:


Buy your gear for your heaviest exposure environment instead of your average day. If you qualify indoors twice a year and spend the rest of your time on patrol, your hardest requirement is an indoor line. In-ear protection you can double up under earmuffs covers both scenarios. If you instruct, your heaviest exposure comes every week, and comfort across eight hours matters more for you.


Take the first week to understand how to fit your gear properly. Seat your earplugs, read a page aloud, and listen for your own voice sounding fuller and closer than usual. That’s what a properly sealed ear canal does to your voice. Try every ear tip size in the box, including a different size in each ear if that is what seals. Wear your hearing protection gear through a full duty day with your helmet and your eye protection on before you take the pair to a range, so you find the pressure points somewhere other than the firing line.


Then build hearing protection into your equipment routine. Charge your earbuds on the same schedule as your radio, and keep a battery-free pair in your kit bag so a flat charge never leaves you with nothing at all.


When you're ready, you can browse[AXIL tactical and military hearing protection](https://goaxil.com/collections/military-and-law-enforcement) , or contact the AXIL team for unit and agency specification.
